To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
every computably enumerable degree bounds exactly one class of 1-generics.
every nonzero c.e. degree can be split by 1-generic degrees, and no two c.e. degrees bound the same classes of 1-generics.
any nonzero computable enumerable degree is 1-generic and that any nonzero computabily enumerable degree can be 1-splitted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to split a computably enumerable degree.
generic splittings of computable and computably enumerable sets.
generic splittings of computable degrees and computably enumerable degrees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for any computably enumerable degree a, the class of degrees bounding the same 1-generic degrees as a is exactly {a}.
there is a 1–1 computably enumerable degree preserving map of the set of computably enumerable 1-generic degrees onto the set of nonzero computably enumerable degrees.
there is no computably enumerable degree bounding the class of 1-generics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the class of 1-generics can be characterized by a certain kind of splitting property.
the 1-generic degrees are the most generic degrees in the sense that they can be split by any other computably enumerable degree.
1-generic splittings are possible for all computably enumerable degrees.
The main takeaway from our work is that
1-genericity is not a computability-theoretic property.
the 1-generics are a much richer class than the computably enumerable degrees and that the 1-generic splitting theorem can be used to prove a number of results in the computably enumerable theory.
1-generics are not “too special” to be used as building blocks for computably enumerable degrees.
